chapter.name: Cell: The Building Block of Life

teaching_strategy: The lesson follows the chapter order. It opens with the hot-spring hook and builds the microscope story first, because that explains why cells stayed unseen. Each topic then alternates explaining, looking at a diagram or photograph, and working a chapter example or activity. Practice questions follow the concept they check and are spread through the deck, and relationship slides tie together ideas that explain each other (resolution to cell size, diffusion to osmosis, ER to Golgi to lysosome, mitosis to meiosis, contact inhibition to cancer). The lesson ends with a concept map of all five topics.

weaknesses: The existing lesson is dense revision notes: the big idea, levels of organisation, resolution, Hooke, microscopes and calculations arrive in one block with no pacing and no single idea per screen.
It has no hook, no picture to explore, no discussion prompt and no practice, so students only read.

Links between ideas (resolution, tiny cells, Hooke, magnification, electron microscope) are listed rather than shown, and the excerpt does not connect the magnification formula to the cell-size activity.
The excerpt stops in the middle of topic 1, so the later topics (osmosis, organelles, cell division, cell theory) get no worked examples or practical activities.
improvements: Open with the Puga Valley hot-spring hook and clear objectives, then teach one or two concepts per slide with a drawn diagram or photograph.
Make the link between resolution and microscopic cells explicit, and turn Activity 2.1 into a worked example that ends with the total-magnification calculation.

Lead each practical (potato in water and salt, Rhoeo and cheek cells in sugar, plant wilting, contact inhibition) into a scenario or application slide, and add relationship slides where one concept explains another.
Spread 23 bank questions through the whole deck right after the concept they check, mostly self-checking (multiple choice, fill in the blanks, flashcards), and end with a concept map.

outline.name: Cell Theory and Regulation of Cell Growth

7309.name: Resolution limit of human eye
7309.definition: At the normal viewing distance of about 25 cm, the human eye cannot distinguish two points closer together than roughly 0.1 mm — they merge into one. This limit is called the resolution of the eye, and it is what makes a microscope necessary rather than merely convenient.

7310.name: Cells are microscopic
7310.definition: Most cells are smaller than 0.1 mm, so they fall below the eye's resolution limit and cannot be seen as separate objects at all. This is why the cell remained unknown until lenses good enough to resolve it were made.

7311.name: Discovery and naming of cell
7311.definition: Robert Hooke first observed and named cells in 1665, examining a thin slice of cork under a simple microscope. He saw tiny empty compartments resembling the cells of a monastery and used that word — so what he actually saw were the dead cell walls, not living cells.

7312.name: Total magnification calculation
7312.definition: The total magnification of a compound microscope is the magnifying power of the eyepiece multiplied by that of the objective lens. A 10× eyepiece with a 40× objective therefore gives 400×, and changing either lens changes the product.

7313.name: Electron microscope advantage
7313.definition: An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons in place of light. Because electrons behave as waves of far shorter wavelength than visible light, it resolves structures at the nanometre scale, which is how organelles inside the cell became visible.

7314.name: Microscope quality features
7314.definition: Microscopes have improved in three respects: resolution, the ability to show two close points as separate; contrast, the difference in brightness that makes a structure stand out; and magnification, the apparent increase in size. Magnification without resolution only produces a bigger blur.

7315.name: Estimating cell size
7315.definition: The size of a cell is estimated by measuring the diameter of the visible field in micrometres and dividing it by the number of cells lying along that diameter. It is an indirect measurement, but it needs no special instrument beyond the microscope itself.

7316.name: Selective permeability of cell membrane
7316.definition: The cell membrane is a thin boundary that encloses the cell and is selectively permeable: it allows some substances through and holds others back. This selectivity is what lets a cell keep its internal composition different from its surroundings.

7317.name: Diffusion along concentration gradient
7317.definition: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration, driven by their random motion. It needs no membrane and no energy from the cell, and it continues until the concentrations are equal.

7318.name: Osmosis across selectively permeable membrane
7318.definition: Osmosis is the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated one. It is a special case of diffusion in which only the water can pass, because the solute particles cannot cross the membrane.

7319.name: Isotonic, hypotonic and hypertonic solutions
7319.definition: A solution is isotonic when its solute concentration equals that inside the cell, so there is no net movement of water; hypotonic when it is lower, so water enters and the cell swells; and hypertonic when it is higher, so water leaves and the cell shrinks.

7320.name: Fluid-mosaic model
7320.definition: The fluid-mosaic model describes the membrane as a double layer of lipid molecules with proteins embedded in it like tiles in a mosaic. The molecules can move sideways, flip and rotate, so the structure is fluid rather than fixed — hence the name.

7321.name: Role of membrane proteins
7321.definition: Proteins embedded in the membrane act as its gatekeepers. Some form channels, others bind a particular substance and carry it across, and it is these proteins rather than the lipid layer that decide which large or charged molecules may enter or leave.

7322.name: Functions of cell wall
7322.definition: Plant, fungal and bacterial cells have a cell wall outside the cell membrane. It is rigid, which gives the cell structural support and shape, but permeable, so it does not control what enters — that remains the work of the membrane.

7323.name: Cell wall maintains plant cell shape
7323.definition: Placed in a concentrated sugar solution a plant cell loses water, and the contents pull away from the wall, but the cell itself does not shrivel. The rigid cell wall holds the original outline, which is why wilted plant tissue recovers its shape when watered.

7324.name: Absence of cell wall in animals
7324.definition: Animal cells have no cell wall, so they can change shape readily. This flexibility is what allows white blood cells to squeeze between other cells, muscle tissue to contract and tissues generally to fold and move.

7325.name: Cell wall is made of cellulose
7325.definition: The plant cell wall is made chiefly of cellulose, a carbohydrate built from long chains of glucose units. Human beings cannot digest cellulose, so in the diet it passes through as roughage and helps the movement of food through the intestine.

7326.name: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
7326.definition: Prokaryotic cells are cells lacking a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, while eukaryotic cells have a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

7327.name: Prokaryotic nucleoid
7327.definition: In a prokaryotic cell the DNA is a single circular molecule lying in a region of the cytoplasm called the nucleoid. It is called a region rather than an organelle precisely because no membrane encloses it.

7328.name: Division of labour in organelles
7328.definition: Eukaryotic organelles divide the work of the cell between them, each carrying out its own process at the same time as the others. The cell therefore runs like a small factory with separate departments rather than as one undifferentiated space.

7329.name: Nucleus and nuclear membrane
7329.definition: The nucleus is enclosed by a double-layered nuclear membrane pierced by pores through which materials pass between nucleus and cytoplasm. Inside lie the nucleolus, where ribosomes are made, and the chromosomes, which carry the cell's genetic information.

7330.name: Chromatin, chromosomes and genes
7330.definition: In a non-dividing cell the genetic material is a diffuse thread-like mass called chromatin; when the cell divides it condenses into distinct chromosomes. Chromosomes are made of DNA with associated proteins, and a gene is a functional segment of that DNA.

7331.name: Ribosomes and protein synthesis
7331.definition: Ribosomes are very small structures, found free in the cytoplasm or attached to the endoplasmic reticulum, and they are the sites at which proteins are assembled. They are present in prokaryotes as well as eukaryotes, since every cell must make proteins.

7332.name: Types of endoplasmic reticulum
7332.definition: Rough endoplasmic reticulum carries ribosomes on its surface and makes proteins destined for secretion or for membranes. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum has no ribosomes and synthesises and stores fats and hormones — the difference in name is a difference in function.

7333.name: Functions of Golgi apparatus
7333.definition: The Golgi apparatus receives proteins and lipids from the endoplasmic reticulum, modifies them, sorts them by destination and packages them into vesicles for transport, secretion, or for forming lysosomes. It is the cell's dispatch department.

7334.name: Lysosomes digest waste materials
7334.definition: Lysosomes are sacs filled with digestive enzymes that break down unwanted proteins, carbohydrates and fats as well as worn-out cell parts. By clearing this material they keep the cell clean, and their enclosure in a membrane keeps their enzymes from digesting the cell itself.

7335.name: Mitochondria supply cellular energy
7335.definition: Mitochondria are double-membrane organelles in which cellular respiration releases energy, stored as ATP. The inner membrane is thrown into folds called cristae, and these folds greatly increase the surface area available for the reactions to take place on.

7336.name: Chloroplasts and photosynthesis
7336.definition: Chloroplasts are double-membrane plastids found in plant cells. They contain the green pigment chlorophyll, which absorbs sunlight, and it is inside them that photosynthesis builds food from carbon dioxide and water.

7337.name: Chromoplasts colour flowers and fruits
7337.definition: Chromoplasts are plastids carrying yellow, orange or red pigments. They give flowers and fruits their bright colours, which serves a purpose for the plant: attracting pollinators to the flower and animals that disperse the seed to the fruit.

7338.name: Leucoplasts store food
7338.definition: Leucoplasts are colourless plastids whose function is storage. They hold reserves of starch, oils or proteins, and they are abundant in storage organs such as potatoes and seeds rather than in green leaves.

7339.name: Vacuoles store and support
7339.definition: A mature plant cell contains one large central vacuole filled with cell sap, which stores water, minerals, sugars and waste products. The pressure it exerts outward against the wall keeps the cell firm, and its loss is what makes a plant wilt.

7340.name: Cytoskeleton supports the cell
7340.definition: The cytoskeleton is a network of fine protein fibres running through the eukaryotic cell. It gives structural support, maintains the cell's shape, anchors organelles, and provides the tracks along which materials are moved inside the cell.

7341.name: DNA in mitochondria and plastids
7341.definition: Mitochondria and plastids contain their own DNA and their own ribosomes and can make some of their own proteins. This is taken as evidence that they descend from free-living bacteria that were engulfed by an early cell and remained within it.

7342.name: Purpose of cell division
7342.definition: Cell division allows an organism to grow by increasing cell number, to repair damaged tissue by replacing lost cells, and to reproduce. In every case new cells come from existing cells, never from non-living material.

7343.name: Regulation by cell cycle
7343.definition: Eukaryotic cells do not divide whenever they can; they pass through an ordered sequence called the cell cycle, with checkpoints at which the cell verifies that conditions and its own DNA are in order before proceeding.

7344.name: Role of mitosis
7344.definition: Mitosis is the commonest form of cell division and serves growth, repair, maintenance and asexual reproduction. Because it preserves the chromosome number exactly, it produces cells that can take the place of those they replace.

7345.name: Role of meiosis
7345.definition: Meiosis occurs only in the reproductive organs and produces gametes. By shuffling the genetic material as it halves the chromosome number, it generates variation among offspring, which is the source of diversity within a species.

7346.name: Result of mitosis
7346.definition: Mitosis yields two daughter cells from one parent cell, each genetically identical to the parent and to each other, with the same DNA and the same chromosome number. This exactness is why mitosis can replace cells without changing the tissue.

7347.name: Result of meiosis
7347.definition: Meiosis consists of two successive divisions and yields four daughter cells, each with half the parental chromosome number. Fertilisation then restores the full number, which is why the chromosome count of a species stays constant across generations.

7348.name: Consequences of faulty cell division
7348.definition: Errors in mitosis can produce uncontrolled division and cells with abnormal chromosome numbers. Errors in meiosis are passed to the offspring and can cause genetic disorders or problems of fertility, because the fault is present in every cell that develops from the gamete.

7349.name: Cell culture method
7349.definition: In cell culture, plant or animal cells are grown outside the body in a sterile, nutrient-rich medium. It allows cells to be studied directly and is used to manufacture biochemicals, medicines and vaccines without using whole organisms.

7350.name: Classical cell theory
7350.definition: The classical cell theory has three statements: all organisms are made of one or more cells; the cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living things; and all cells arise from pre-existing cells. The third of these ruled out spontaneous generation.

7351.name: Definite life span of cells
7351.definition: Every cell has a definite life span: it grows and divides in a controlled way, performs its function, and dies when it is no longer needed. The dead cells are removed and replaced, so a tissue stays the same while its cells are continually renewed.

7352.name: Contact inhibition
7352.definition: Contact inhibition is the property by which many animal cells stop dividing once they touch neighbouring cells. It is what keeps a tissue to its proper size and stops a healing wound from growing past the point where the gap has closed.

7353.name: Cancer and uncontrolled division
7353.definition: Cancer cells lose contact inhibition and continue dividing without restraint, forming a tumour. Such cells may invade the tissues around them and spread to other parts of the body, which is what makes cancer dangerous rather than the growth itself.

7354.name: Programmed cell death
7354.definition: Programmed cell death is the deliberate, genetically regulated destruction of selected cells. It is needed in normal development — it removes the webbing between a developing embryo's fingers — and it serves quality control and the immune system by eliminating damaged or infected cells.

7355.name: Totipotency of plant cells
7355.definition: Totipotency is the ability of a single living plant cell to develop into a complete plant when given suitable nutrients and conditions. It is the basis of plant tissue culture, by which a whole plant can be raised from a small piece of tissue.

Conditions like Earth 3.5 billion years ago
content.example: Scientists from the Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences found that calcium carbonate formed rapidly around the springs. These deposits may have protected early organic molecules from harmful radiation and extreme conditions, and may have helped form the first protective membrane.

slides.title: Why most cells cannot be seen

relationship.idea: The 0.1 mm limit of resolution of the eye is the yardstick that shows why cells, mostly smaller than 0.1 mm, stay invisible and why a microscope is necessary.

explanations.text: Two points closer than 0.1 mm, viewed from 25 cm, merge into one: the eye's limit of resolution.
Most cells are too small for the unaided eye, so they cannot be seen without a microscope.

content.example: Typical cells measure 1 to 10 µm (bacterial) or 10 to 100 µm (eukaryotic), and 1 mm = 1000 µm.
content.relationship_note: The 0.1 mm limit of the eye is the yardstick: cells fall below it, so a microscope is needed to see them.
content.key_idea: The eye cannot separate points closer than 0.1 mm, and cells are usually smaller, so we need a microscope.

interaction.intro: Follow the two-dot thought experiment one step at a time.

items.label: Two dots, far apart
items.text: Draw two tiny dots on paper and look at them from about 25 cm, the near point of the human eye. While they are well apart, you see two.

items.label: Move them closer
items.text: Slide the dots together. Nothing about the dots changes, but the gap between them shrinks until the eye can no longer register it.

items.label: They merge
items.text: At about 0.1 mm apart, the two points appear as one. This is the limit of resolution: the eye's ability to see very close objects as separate and distinct.

items.label: Cells fall below it
items.text: A cell is usually too small to be seen by the unaided eye. That raises the question of how cell biologists studied structures much smaller than this limit.

items.label: Lenses extend the eye
items.text: A convex lens, or an objective lens combined with an eyepiece, makes an object appear larger. That is the tool that answers the question.

interaction.wrapup: The eye sets the limit, and lenses are how that limit was crossed.

slides.title: Hooke looks at cork and names the cell

explanations.text: Robert Hooke first observed a cell in 1665, in a thin slice of cork, and named the small box-like compartments 'cells'.

content.example: Hooke used a self-designed microscope capable of about 200–300X magnification.
content.key_idea: Robert Hooke was the first person to observe a cell, in 1665.

discussion.prompt: Why could Hooke see the compartments in cork through his microscope when nobody could see them with the naked eye?
discussion.answer: A cell is usually too small for the unaided eye to resolve. His lenses made the object appear larger, so the compartments could be seen.

items.label: Hooke names the cell
items.text: Using a self-designed microscope, Hooke looks at a thin slice of cork and names its box-like compartments cells. Every later step starts from this sighting.

items.label: Schleiden and plants
items.text: German botanist Matthias Schleiden reports that all plants are made up of cells.

items.label: Schwann and animals
items.text: German zoologist Theodor Schwann finds that all animals are also made up of cells, so cells now cover both plants and animals.

items.label: Virchow and new cells
items.text: German scientist Rudolf Virchow expands the Cell Theory by stating that new cells are formed only from pre-existing cells.

interaction.wrapup: Together, their work led to the formulation of the Cell Theory.

slides.title: Total magnification: eyepiece times objective

explanations.text: Total magnification is the eyepiece's magnifying power multiplied by the objective lens's magnifying power.

content.example: A 10X eyepiece with a 10X objective gives 100X, so an onion cell of estimated size 200 µm appears 100 times larger.
content.key_idea: Total magnification equals eyepiece power multiplied by objective lens power.

discussion.prompt: If you kept the 10X eyepiece but switched to a 40X objective lens, what would happen to the total magnification, and why?
discussion.answer: It would rise to 400X, because the two powers are multiplied, so changing either lens changes the product.

interaction.intro: Open the steps in order to see how total magnification is built.

items.label: Start with the eyepiece
items.text: Total magnification depends on the magnifying power of the eyepiece and of the objective lens. Start with the eyepiece: its power is the first of the two numbers you need.

items.label: Add the objective lens
items.text: School light microscopes offer different objective lenses, such as 10X and 40X, to achieve better magnification and resolution under visible light. The objective in use gives the second number.

items.label: Multiply the two powers
items.text: Because total magnification is a product, changing either the eyepiece or the objective lens changes the total.

items.label: Remember what it gives you
items.text: What you see is a magnified image of the object, not a statement of its size. To find the actual size you estimate it separately, as in Activity 2.1.

interaction.wrapup: Two numbers and one multiplication give the magnification. The actual size of a cell needs a different measurement.

slides.title: Estimating the size of an onion cell

explanations.text: Estimate a cell's real size: divide the diameter of the visible field in micrometres by the number of cells along it.

content.example: Read a 5 mm field on a ruler: 5 × 1000 = 5000 µm, since 1 mm = 1000 µm. Swap in an onion peel slide and count 25 cells in one straight line: 5000 µm / 25 = 200 µm per cell.

slides.title: From diffusion to osmosis

relationship.idea: Osmosis is diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane, so it needs both the concentration-gradient idea and the selective membrane.

explanations.text: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration, even without a membrane.
Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane, from a dilute to a concentrated solution.

content.example: Dye spreads through water and fragrance through air by diffusion. In plants, water from the soil enters root cells by osmosis.
content.relationship_note: Osmosis is diffusion of water, so it needs both a concentration difference and a selectively permeable membrane.
content.key_idea: Water keeps moving until the concentrations on the two sides become equal.

interaction.intro: Select each part of the diagram to follow the water.

spots.label: Dilute solution: more water, less solute
spots.text: Water leaves from this side. The difference in concentration between the two sides, called a concentration gradient, is what sets the movement going, just as it does for any particles that intermix.

spots.label: Selectively permeable membrane
spots.text: It lets water move in and out but not the sugar or salt molecules. Diffusion occurs even without a membrane; osmosis is specifically the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable one.

spots.label: Concentrated solution: less water, more solute
spots.text: Water arrives on this side, which has less water and more solute. Because the solute cannot cross the membrane, water is the only thing that moves, and it moves from dilute toward concentrated.

spots.label: Concentrations become equal
spots.text: Water keeps moving until the concentrations in the two areas become equal. That balanced state is the idea behind the term isotonic, which you meet next.

interaction.wrapup: Water moves from the dilute side to the concentrated side through a membrane that holds back the solute, until both sides match.

concepts: Cell wall maintains plant cell shape

slides.title: Plant and animal cells in sugar solution
concepts: Absence of cell wall in animals
Cell wall is made of cellulose

relationship.idea: Plant cells are held in shape by a wall of cellulose, while animal cells lack a wall and can change shape easily.

explanations.text: Animal cells have no cell wall, so they change shape easily, supporting movement of tissues.
The plant cell wall is mainly cellulose, a carbohydrate made of many linked glucose units.

content.example: In 20 per cent sugar solution, Rhoeo cells keep their boundaries but cheek cells shrink considerably. Cellulose in our diet acts as roughage, helping digestion.
content.relationship_note: Plant cells are held in shape by a wall of cellulose, while animal cells lack a wall and change shape easily.
content.key_idea: Whether a cell has a wall decides if it keeps its shape when it loses water.

interaction.situation: Imagine a Rhoeo leaf cell whose wall has become as flexible as a cell membrane. You place it in 20 per cent sugar solution beside a normal Rhoeo cell and a cheek cell, and look again after half an hour.

nodes.prompt: Water leaves all three cells by osmosis. What will the outline of the flexible-walled cell do?

choices.text: Its outline shrinks along with its contents, like the cheek cell
choices.outcome: The whole cell draws in. With no rigid wall to resist, its boundary follows the contents inward, just as the cheek cell's does.
choices.why: The normal Rhoeo cell keeps its boundary because its rigid wall holds the shape while the membrane pulls away inside. A flexible wall could not do that.

choices.text: Its outline stays the same, because plant cells always keep their shape
choices.outcome: Not quite. Only a rigid wall holds the outline fixed. A wall as flexible as a membrane gives way, so the cell would shrink.
choices.why: Shape is held by the rigidity of the wall, not by the cell simply being a plant cell. Cheek cells shrink considerably because they have no wall to resist.

nodes.prompt: Now picture a whole plant built from such cells, fixed in one place through wind and rain. What would the flexible walls cost it?

choices.text: It would struggle to stay upright and keep its leaves and flowers firm
choices.outcome: The rigid wall is what lets leaves and flowers stay firm and the plant stand upright. With flexible walls it could not withstand wind and rain.
choices.why: Plants cannot move away from stress, so they rely on a rigid wall made mainly of cellulose. Animal cells can change shape easily, which supports the movement of tissues.

choices.text: Nothing, because the cell membrane already protects the cell enough
choices.outcome: The membrane defines the cell and controls what passes through, but it is only about 7 to 10 nanometres thick and cannot give a plant rigid support.
choices.why: Protection and rigidity are different jobs. The wall is the additional covering that plants, fungi and bacteria have, giving protection and structural support.

interaction.conclusion: Rigidity and flexibility are a trade-off. Plants, usually fixed in one place, gain firm shape from a cellulose wall. Animal cells have no wall and change shape easily, which supports the movement of tissues.

slides.title: The cell as a tiny living factory

explanations.text: Eukaryotic organelles carry out different life processes independently and at the same time, building materials, removing waste and providing energy.

content.example: The chapter's factory labels: ribosomes are the protein factories, the Golgi apparatus is the post office, lysosomes are the clean-up system and mitochondria are the powerhouses.
content.key_idea: A cell is like a tiny living factory, with each part doing a specific job.

discussion.prompt: Prokaryotic cells carry out most activities directly in the cytoplasm. What might eukaryotic cells gain from having separate organelles?
discussion.answer: Different processes can run independently at the same time, like departments in a factory, so building, waste removal and energy supply all go on together.

interaction.intro: Select each department to see its job in the cell factory.

spots.label: Nucleus
spots.text: The house of coded instructions. Its chromosomes carry the cell's genetic information as DNA. Its nucleolus makes ribosomal subunits, which exit to the cytoplasm and assemble into ribosomes.

spots.label: Ribosomes
spots.text: The protein factories. Some float freely in the cytoplasm and some attach to the endoplasmic reticulum; both are sites of protein synthesis. Each forms from one large and one small subunit.

spots.label: Endoplasmic reticulum
spots.text: The manufacturing factory: a network spreading through the cytoplasm, continuous with the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope. It makes and transports proteins, fats and some hormones in specialised cells.

spots.label: Golgi apparatus
spots.text: The cell's post office: stacks of flattened sacs linked to the ER, the cell membrane and other organelles. It modifies, sorts and packages proteins or lipids into vesicles.

spots.label: Lysosomes
spots.text: The clean-up system: single membrane-bound sacs of enzymes that break down unwanted proteins, carbohydrates, fats and damaged parts. The breakdown products enter the cytoplasm, where they may be reused.

spots.label: Mitochondria
spots.text: The powerhouses: glucose and other molecules are broken down here in cellular respiration, and the energy released is stored as ATP, the energy currency used for most cellular activities.

interaction.wrapup: Every department works at the same time, and the products of one feed the next, so the cell runs as one coordinated system.

slides.title: The nucleus and its genetic material

relationship.idea: Chromatin, chromosomes and genes all lie inside the nucleus, which is the compartment that holds the cell's genetic information.

items.label: Double membrane with pores

items.label: Nucleolus

items.label: Chromatin and chromosomes

items.label: Genes
items.text: Genes are the functional segments of DNA. Chromosomes carry the information for inheritance of characters from parents to the next generation, and that information is held in the DNA molecules.

items.label: DNA in action

spots.text: Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork through a microscope he designed himself, magnifying about 200 to 300 times. He saw small box-like compartments and called them cells.

spots.label: Schleiden: plants are cells, 1838
spots.text: Matthias Schleiden, a German botanist, reported that all plants are made up of cells. This covered plants only; the animal case came a year later.

spots.label: Schwann: animals are cells, 1839
spots.text: Theodor Schwann, a German zoologist, found that all animals are also made up of cells. With plants and animals both covered, cells became something shared by living things.

spots.label: Virchow: new cells from pre-existing cells, 1855
spots.text: Rudolf Virchow, a German scientist, expanded the theory by stating that new cells are formed only from pre-existing cells. This added where cells come from, not only what organisms are made of.

spots.label: Classical cell theory
spots.text: Together, this work formed three statements. The theory unifies all biology, from bacteria to humans, and its last statement explains life's continuity through cell division.

interaction.wrapup: Each observation added one piece: what cells are, which organisms have them, and where new cells come from.

slides.section: Cell Theory and Regulation of Cell Growth
slides.title: Every cell has a life span

explanations.text: Each cell grows and divides in a controlled way, does its work and dies when no longer needed; new cells replace it.

content.example: Mature red blood cells have no nucleus, so they cannot repair or divide themselves. They survive about 120 days.
content.key_idea: Cells that do not die when they should, or die too early, cause problems.

discussion.prompt: Why does the body need cells to die as well as to divide?
discussion.answer: Cells die when they are no longer needed and new cells carry out the same function. If cells fail to die on time or die too early, problems can arise in the body.

interaction.intro: Put these stages of a cell's life span in order.

items.text: A cell grows and divides in a controlled way
It stays in the right place and carries out its function
It dies when it is no longer needed
A new cell doing the same function replaces it

interaction.wrapup: Every day almost 1 per cent of your cells are replaced. If cells fail to die when they should, or die too early, problems arise in the body.

slides.section: Cell Theory and Regulation of Cell Growth
slides.title: Growth with and without the brakes

relationship.idea: Cancer is what follows when the contact inhibition that holds a tissue to its proper size is lost.

explanations.text: In contact inhibition, many animal cells stop dividing once they touch neighbouring cells.
Cancer cells lose this control and keep dividing uncontrollably, forming tumours.

content.example: A tumour may be benign or malignant. Cancerous tumours can invade nearby tissues and spread to other parts of the body, forming new tumours.
content.relationship_note: Cancer is what follows when contact inhibition, which stops cells dividing once they touch neighbours, is lost.
content.key_idea: Cells that touch normally stop dividing; cancer cells lose this brake and keep dividing.

interaction.situation: Animal cells in a tissue are dividing. As they spread, each one begins to touch its neighbouring cells. Follow what normal cells do, then what happens when one cell loses that control.

nodes.prompt: Normal cells now touch their neighbours. What do they do?

choices.text: They keep dividing, since dividing is how tissues grow.
choices.outcome: That is the behaviour of cancer cells, not of normal cells. Normal cells respond to the touch of a neighbour.
choices.why: Growth does come from division, but it is controlled. Division usually stops when cells come in contact with neighbouring cells.

choices.outcome: Division halts once the cells touch. This is called contact inhibition.
choices.why: Many animal cells stop dividing when they contact neighbouring cells, which keeps growth controlled.

nodes.prompt: Now one cell loses contact inhibition. What does it do when it touches its neighbours?

choices.text: It stops dividing anyway, because its neighbours have stopped.
choices.outcome: It does not stop. A cell without contact inhibition does not respond to the touch of its neighbours.
choices.why: Cancer cells lose this control and keep dividing uncontrollably, whatever the cells around them are doing.

choices.text: It carries on dividing without restraint.
choices.outcome: Its descendants keep dividing too, and the growing mass of cells forms a tumour.
choices.why: Cells that lose contact inhibition keep dividing uncontrollably, which leads to the formation of tumours.

interaction.conclusion: Touching neighbours switches division off in many animal cells. A cell that loses this control keeps dividing and forms a tumour. Plant cells, with rigid cell walls, do not show contact inhibition and follow a different pattern of growth.

slides.section: Cell Theory and Regulation of Cell Growth
slides.title: Programmed cell death

explanations.text: Programmed cell death is the genetically regulated, organised destruction of selected cells, needed for development, quality control and immune function.

content.example: When an embryo develops, programmed cell death helps form fingers by eliminating the cells between the digits. Without it we would have webbed hands.
content.key_idea: Cells also have natural ways of dying to maintain a balance.

interaction.intro: Open each card to see how three controls keep the number of cells in balance.

items.label: Cell division
items.text: Adds cells. Cells divide to replace old, dead or damaged cells, so the body can grow and repair itself.

items.label: Contact inhibition
items.text: Stops the adding. In many animal cells, division usually stops when cells touch neighbouring cells, so a tissue does not keep growing.

items.label: Programmed cell death
items.text: Removes cells. Genes direct the destruction of selected cells in an organised way, so the body can shape itself and remove cells it does not need.

interaction.wrapup: Division adds cells, contact inhibition stops the adding, and programmed death removes cells; together they keep numbers in balance.

slides.section: Cell Theory and Regulation of Cell Growth
slides.title: One plant cell, a whole plant

explanations.text: Totipotency is the ability of a single living plant cell to develop into a complete plant, the basis of plant tissue culture.

content.example: In 1902, Gottlieb Haberlandt proposed that even a fully mature cell from a permanent tissue can form a complete plant if given suitable nutrients and favourable conditions.
content.key_idea: A living plant cell can form different types of cells, so one cell can give a whole plant.

interaction.intro: Open each card to see what the idea of totipotency includes.

items.label: Any living plant cell
items.text: The idea covers even a fully mature cell from a permanent tissue. Haberlandt suggested plant cells can form different types of cells and also change them, so a cell is not locked into one job.

items.label: It needs the right conditions
items.text: A cell alone is not enough. It needs suitable nutrients and favourable conditions, which echoes cell culture, where cells grow in a nutrient-rich medium.

items.label: A new field of biology
items.text: The idea laid the foundation for a new branch of biology known as Plant Tissue Culture Technology, in which a whole plant can be raised from a small piece of tissue.

interaction.wrapup: Given the right medium, a single living plant cell can develop into a complete plant.

slides.title: Concept map: how the cell fits together

content.body: Link the five parts of the chapter into one picture.
content.key_idea: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms.

discussion.prompt: How do the cell membrane, the organelles and cell division work together to keep an organism alive?
discussion.answer: The membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell. Organelles build new materials, remove waste and provide energy. Cell division replaces old, dead or damaged cells.

interaction.intro: Select each part of the map to see how it connects to the rest of the chapter.

spots.label: How to study cells
spots.text: Cells are usually too small for the unaided eye, whose limit of resolution is 0.1 mm. Microscopes, from Hooke's in 1665 to electron microscopes, opened up everything else in the chapter.

spots.label: Cell membrane and cell wall
spots.text: Every cell has a selectively permeable membrane, so osmosis explains why cells swell or shrink. Plant, fungi and bacteria cells add a wall, which keeps plant cells in shape when water leaves.

spots.label: Cell interior and organelles
spots.text: Inside, the cytoplasm and nucleus, plus organelles in eukaryotic cells, share the work like a tiny living factory. Prokaryotic cells lack a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

spots.label: Cell division
spots.text: Mitosis makes identical body cells for growth and repair. Meiosis makes gametes with half the chromosomes, and fertilisation restores the full number. Errors in either cause problems.

spots.label: Cell theory and regulation of cell growth
spots.text: The theory says all cells arise from pre-existing cells, which is why division matters. Contact inhibition and programmed cell death keep growth balanced, and every cell has a definite life span.

interaction.wrapup: Each part answers a different question about one unit: the cell, the basic unit of structure and function in living things.
